analogy.p: Bacteria are like burglars who move into a warm house, multiply quickly, and break things and leave a mess (toxins). A virus is like a squatter who cannot survive without the house's machinery: it forces the house to produce copies of the squatter, and the walls are wrecked as they leave. It breaks down because bacteria are real living cells that can act alone, whereas viruses are not cells at all.

bullets: **Pathogen** = a microorganism that causes disease.
**Communicable (infectious) disease** = a disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.
Four types of pathogen: **bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists**.
Pathogens can infect **both plants and animals**.
Three spread routes named in the spec: **direct contact, water, air**.
Two ways illness is caused: **rapid reproduction in the body** and **damage by toxins or to cells**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.3.1 (Communicable diseases) states that **pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease**. Pathogens may be **viruses, bacteria, protists or fungi**. They may infect plants or animals and can be **spread by direct contact, by water or by air**. You must also know how bacteria and viruses actually make you ill: they **reproduce rapidly inside the body**, **bacteria may produce toxins** that damage tissues, and **viruses live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage**. Everything else in the topic (spread, defences, vaccines, drugs) builds on these basics.

bullets: Communicable examples: measles, HIV, malaria, salmonella food poisoning, gonorrhoea, tobacco mosaic virus, rose black spot.
Non-communicable examples: coronary heart disease, most cancers, type 2 diabetes, asthma, lung disease linked to smoking.
Non-communicable diseases are usually linked to lifestyle, genes, age or the environment, not to infection.
Some diseases have several causes (for example some cancers are triggered by a virus), so always check the question wording.
The words **infectious**, **contagious** and **communicable** are used loosely to mean the disease can spread.
Plants can also suffer communicable diseases (TMV, rose black spot) and non-communicable problems (mineral deficiency).
core.p: A **communicable disease** is caused by a pathogen and can be passed on, directly or indirectly, from one organism to another. A **non-communicable disease** is not caused by a pathogen and **cannot be passed on**. Examiners often ask you to give an example of each, or to say why a disease such as cancer cannot spread from person to person like flu. The key idea is simple: if there is no pathogen, there is nothing to transmit.

bullets: Many bacteria reproduce by **binary fission** (one cell splits into two) as often as every 20 minutes in warm, moist conditions with nutrients.
The human body is warm, moist and full of nutrients, so it is an ideal place for bacteria to grow.
Pathogenic bacteria cause illness by **damaging cells** and by **producing toxins**.
Bacterial diseases in the spec: **salmonella** and **gonorrhoea**.
Bacteria can be killed by **antibiotics** (viruses cannot).
Not all bacteria are pathogens: say "some bacteria", never "bacteria cause disease".
core.h: Bacteria: structure and what makes them harmful
core.p: **Bacteria** are single-celled **prokaryotes**: they have cytoplasm, a cell membrane and a cell wall but **no nucleus**; their genetic material is a single DNA loop with extra small rings called plasmids, lying free in the cytoplasm. Most bacteria are harmless or useful (gut bacteria help digestion, others make yoghurt), but pathogenic bacteria cause disease. They are about 0.001 to 0.01 mm long, so they are visible only with a microscope but are far larger than viruses.

bullets: No cell membrane, nucleus or cytoplasm, so a virus cannot divide by binary fission.
A virus must **hijack the host cell** so the cell copies the viral genetic material and makes new virus protein.
Viruses are **not killed by antibiotics**; control relies on vaccination, hygiene and (for HIV) antiviral drugs.
They infect animals, plants and even bacteria.
A single virus particle can lead to hundreds or thousands of new particles from one infected cell.
Because viruses live inside cells, they are hard to treat without harming the host cell.
core.h: Viruses: structure and how they are different
core.p: **Viruses** are much smaller than bacteria (often about 100 times smaller). A virus is a piece of genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a **protein coat**; it is **not a cell**, has no cytoplasm and cannot carry out life processes by itself. It can only reproduce **inside a living host cell**, which is why it is described as an obligate parasite. Viral diseases in the spec include **measles, HIV and tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)**.

bullets: Step 1: the virus **attaches** to a host cell with a shape that fits a receptor on the surface.
Step 2: the virus (or its genetic material) **enters** the cell.
Step 3: the cell's machinery is **taken over** to copy the viral genetic material and make virus proteins.
Step 4: many **new virus particles** are assembled.
Step 5: the new viruses **leave the cell**, often by bursting it (lysis), and go on to infect more cells.
Cell damage means tissues cannot work properly, which is why symptoms appear.
core.h: How viruses cause illness: replication inside cells
core.p: Viruses cause harm because they **live and reproduce inside cells, causing cell damage**. The virus attaches to a specific host cell, gets its genetic material inside, and uses the cell's own ribosomes, enzymes and energy to make many copies of itself. When the new viruses are released the host cell is often damaged or destroyed, and the body's symptoms (fever, rash, tiredness) come from the damage and from the immune response.

bullets: Rapid growth: the bacteria share your nutrients and warmth and keep dividing.
Toxins damage cells and tissues; in food poisoning they irritate the gut lining, causing vomiting and diarrhoea.
The immune response (high temperature, inflammation) also contributes to symptoms.
Larger populations release more toxin, so more severe symptoms follow.
Treating early with antibiotics (for a bacterial disease) stops the numbers growing.
Link: white blood cells and antibodies fight this growth (see human defence systems).
core.h: How bacteria cause illness: rapid reproduction and toxins
core.p: Bacteria cause illness through two linked processes. First they **reproduce rapidly inside the body**, so numbers rise from a few cells to millions in hours. Second, many bacteria **produce toxins (poisons) that damage tissues and make us feel ill**. Some bacteria also directly damage the cells they live on. Symptoms normally appear only once the population is big enough, and that is why there is a delay (the incubation period) between infection and feeling ill.

bullets: Fungi and protists are **eukaryotes**: their cells have a nucleus.
Rose black spot (fungus) makes leaves spotty, reducing photosynthesis.
Malaria (protist) is carried from person to person by a vector, the mosquito.
A **vector** is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without usually being ill itself.
Fungicides treat fungal diseases; antibiotics do not work on fungi.
Athlete's foot is another fungal infection, though only rose black spot is named in the spec.
core.p: **Fungi** can be single-celled (yeast) or made of thread-like **hyphae**. Fungal pathogens grow on or in a host and absorb nutrients from it, damaging the tissue. **Protists** are eukaryotic, mostly single-celled organisms, and some are parasites. The spec example for protists is **malaria**, which is spread by an organism called a vector. The spec example for fungi is **rose black spot**, which infects plants.

bullets: **Direct contact**: touching an infected person or surface (and sexual contact, e.g. gonorrhoea, HIV).
**Air**: droplet infection, e.g. measles and flu, spread by coughs and sneezes.
**Water**: contaminated drinking or bathing water, e.g. cholera.
Plants: pathogens spread by wind, water, soil, insects, and direct contact between leaves.
Spread is reduced by hygiene, isolation, vaccination and killing vectors (see spread and prevention).
The more people packed together, the faster a disease spreads.
core.h: How pathogens spread: direct contact, water and air
core.p: The specification says pathogens "can be spread by **direct contact**, by **water** or by **air**". In direct contact you pass the pathogen by touching, by sexual contact or through body fluids such as blood. Water can carry bacteria and other pathogens if it is contaminated by sewage. Air carries tiny droplets released by coughs and sneezes, which another person breathes in. Food can also carry pathogens, as with salmonella.

bullets: Number of divisions = total time ÷ time for one division.
Number of bacteria = starting number × 2^(number of divisions).
Example: dividing every 20 minutes for 2 hours = 6 divisions, so 1 bacterium becomes 2^6 = 64.
Check units: convert hours to minutes before dividing.
Real growth levels off as food runs out and waste builds up, so the curve does not rise for ever.
Link to microbiology practical: counting colonies on agar plates uses similar ideas.
core.h: Exponential growth and the maths of bacterial numbers
core.p: Because a bacterium splits in two, the population **doubles** every division. After n divisions one bacterium becomes **2^n** bacteria. This is **exponential growth** and is why a tiny infection can become serious so fast. A common exam skill is to be given a division time and a total time, work out the number of divisions, then calculate the population.

bullets: TMV produces a mosaic of discoloured patches on leaves.
Discoloured leaf areas lack chloroplasts so photosynthesis falls.
Rose black spot spreads by wind and water splash.
Aphids and other insects can act as vectors for plant pathogens.
Plants have physical defences (waxy cuticle, cell walls, bark) and chemical defences.
Link: triple biology covers detection and identification of plant disease.
core.p: Plants are infected by viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists too. Plant disease reduces growth because damaged leaves cannot photosynthesise, and this affects crop yield and food security. The specification examples are **tobacco mosaic virus** and **rose black spot**.

bullets: Cell biology: bacteria are prokaryotes; fungi and protists are eukaryotes.
Human defence systems: phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxins respond directly to rapid reproduction and toxins.
Vaccination: a safe form of the pathogen trains memory lymphocytes.
Antibiotics: kill bacteria, not viruses, because they target bacterial structures.
Evolution: resistant bacteria arise by natural selection.
Health: alcohol, smoking and diet cause non-communicable disease.
core.p: This opening point is the foundation of 4.3. Later points explain how disease spread is limited, how white blood cells and antibodies kill pathogens, why vaccination works, and how antibiotics treat bacterial but not viral disease. It also links to cell biology (prokaryote and eukaryote cells), to ecology (parasites) and to health (non-communicable diseases such as heart disease).

bullets: Chain structure: cause → effect → symptom.
Compare bacteria and viruses using the same features (size, cell structure, reproduction, treatment).
Explain why a virus cannot be treated with antibiotics: it lives inside cells and has no bacterial structures to attack.
Explain why symptoms are delayed: numbers must reach a threshold.
Use data: infection rate graphs rising fast suggest rapid reproduction.
If asked "how does it spread" name the route and the mechanism (e.g. droplets inhaled).
core.h: Higher-tier style thinking: explaining, not just stating
core.p: Higher questions reward links using "because" and "so". For example: "Bacteria multiply rapidly **so** toxin concentration rises **which** damages cells **so** symptoms appear." Always say what the pathogen does, what that does to the body, and what the result is. Use the exact terms pathogen, toxin, reproduce, host cell, and tissue damage.

exam: **1 mark: define** - "A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease." Say "microorganism" and "disease".
**State** the four types of pathogen: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists (4 marks if asked for all, 1 each).
**2 marks: how bacteria make you ill** - (1) reproduce rapidly inside the body; (2) produce toxins that damage tissues.
**2 marks: how viruses make you ill** - (1) live and reproduce inside cells; (2) which damages / destroys the cells.
**Give two ways pathogens spread** - direct contact, water, air; add an example for the second mark.
**Explain (3 to 4 marks)** - use a chain: cause, effect, symptom, and use "so/because".
**Compare bacteria and virus (4 marks)** - give a feature of both in each point (size, cell structure, reproduction, antibiotics).
**Calculation** - show divisions = time ÷ doubling time, then 2^n; write the working to earn method marks.
**Graph questions** - a steep rise in cases shows rapid reproduction/spread; quote numbers from the axis.
**Avoid vague words** - write "damage tissue" rather than "make you sick"; "microorganism" rather than "germ".

mistakes.r: Pathogens may be bacteria, viruses, fungi or protists.
Viruses reproduce only inside living host cells, using the cell's machinery.
Only some bacteria are pathogens; many are harmless or useful.
Antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses (viruses live inside cells).
They reproduce rapidly and produce toxins that damage tissues.
mistakes.w: Bacteria make you ill because they eat your cells.

mistakes.r: A pathogen is the microorganism that causes the disease.
Cancer is non-communicable; it is not caused by a pathogen and cannot be passed on.
A virus is not a cell: it is genetic material in a protein coat.

summary: AQA wants you to define a pathogen and communicable disease, name the four types of pathogen, state how pathogens spread (direct contact, water, air) and explain how bacteria (rapid reproduction and toxins) and viruses (reproducing inside and damaging cells) cause illness. It matters because the whole of infection and response builds on these ideas.

terms.d: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be spread from one organism to another.
A disease that cannot be passed from one organism to another; not caused by a pathogen.
Single-celled prokaryote microorganisms without a nucleus; some are pathogens.
A tiny pathogen made of genetic material in a protein coat that can only reproduce inside living cells.
A eukaryotic organism, single-celled (yeast) or made of hyphae, some of which are pathogens.
A eukaryotic, mainly single-celled organism; some are pathogens, e.g. the one that causes malaria.
A poison produced by bacteria that damages tissues and makes us feel ill.
The organism that a pathogen lives in or on.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.
Asexual reproduction in which one bacterial cell divides into two.
Spread of a pathogen by touching an infected organism or its fluids.
Spread of pathogens in tiny droplets from coughs and sneezes that are breathed in.
Another term for a communicable disease caused by a pathogen.
A sign of illness that the patient experiences, such as fever or rash.

worked.ans: Bacteria reproduce rapidly inside the body (1). They release toxins (1) that damage body tissues and make the person feel ill (1).
worked.q: Explain how bacteria can make a person feel ill. (3 marks)
steps: Mark 1: bacteria reproduce rapidly inside the body.
Mark 3: the toxins damage cells/tissues, causing symptoms.

worked.q: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria will there be after 3 hours? (3 marks)

worked.ans: A virus is not a cell, but a bacterium is a single-celled organism (1). A virus can reproduce only inside a host cell, whereas bacteria can divide by themselves (1). (Also: viruses are smaller; antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses.)
worked.q: Give two differences between a virus and a bacterium. (2 marks)
steps: Structure: virus not a cell; bacterium is a (prokaryotic) cell.
Reproduction: virus only inside host cells; bacteria divide on their own.
